summary: Learners compare experimental probability (relative frequency measured from actual trials) with theoretical probability (calculated from equally-likely outcomes). The central idea is a child-level law of large numbers: as the number of trials grows, the experimental relative frequency tends toward the theoretical value, while short runs can differ widely and each trial stays independent. Learners run trials, compute relative frequency from their OWN tally (frequency ÷ number of trials), and compare with prediction — and they confront two common fallacies: that experimental results should equal theory exactly, and that outcomes become 'due' or that absolute counts catch up to be equal.
misconceptions: Expecting experimental results to equal the theoretical probability, and calling a device biased after a short run (law of small numbers)
Thinking absolute counts 'catch up' to become exactly equal with more trials (gambler's fallacy of convergence / the 'due' idea)
Reporting the theoretical probability when asked for the experimental one (or vice versa)
Trusting a small sample as much as a large one to estimate an unknown probability

activities.title: Roll, tally, and compute your own experimental probability
steps: Roll a die 60 times (or flip a coin / spin a spinner), tallying each result in a frequency table.
Add a relative-frequency column: for each outcome compute frequency ÷ 60 as a fraction or decimal.
State the theoretical probability (1/6 for a fair die) and mark both the experimental and theoretical values on the same 0-to-1 scale.
Write in your own words how your experimental values compare with 1/6, and whether the differences you see are enough to call the die unfair.
activities.insight: Experimental probability comes from the data you collected (f ÷ n); it is usually close to but not exactly the theoretical value, and ordinary short-run differences are expected rather than proof of bias.

activities.title: Short run vs long run: watch the proportion settle while counts stay unequal
steps: Compare your own short run (60 rolls) with a much longer run — pool the whole class's tallies, or use a trials simulator set to 60, then 600, then 6000.
At each trial count, record both the relative frequency for each outcome AND the raw counts.
Predict before increasing the trials: 'If I roll 600 times instead of 60, will each number come up exactly 100 times?' Then check against the data.

Describe what gets closer to what: check whether, at the largest trial count, the relative frequencies for a fair die all sit near 1/6 (or near the theoretical value for your coin or spinner), while the raw counts (for example 995 vs 1020) are still unequal.
activities.insight: It is the PROPORTION (relative frequency) that converges toward the theoretical value with more trials — not the absolute counts becoming equal. No outcome is ever 'due', and each trial is independent of the ones before it.

activities.title: Judge a fairness claim from sample size
steps: Read a scenario: 'A 4 came up 14 times in 60 rolls of a die.' Decide whether this proves the die is biased, and explain your reasoning.
Decide whose data you would trust more to estimate the chance of an outcome for a possibly-bent coin: 20 flips or 500 flips, and say why.
Order several sample sizes from least to most reliable for estimating an unknown probability.
Explain how you WOULD decide, with much more confidence, whether the die is loaded — and why even many trials give strong evidence rather than absolute certainty.
activities.insight: A small sample is not as trustworthy as a large one for estimating an unknown probability; a single ordinary deviation over few trials is not evidence of bias, and judging fairness sensibly depends on the number of trials behind the data.

checkQuestion: Give the child a die and have them roll it 60 times, tallying each result. Then say: 'Work out the experimental probability of each number from your results. How do they compare with what you'd expect for a fair die? And what would you expect if you rolled 600 times instead of 60?' (Set the task and WATCH — watch whether they compute relative frequency from THEIR data or just state 1/6, whether they treat a deviation as proof of bias, and whether they think 600 rolls would give exactly 100 each.)
checkAnswer: A correct performance: computes each experimental probability as that number's frequency ÷ 60 from the actual tally, notes the values are close to but not exactly 1/6, explains the differences as normal short-run variation, and predicts that 600 rolls would bring the relative frequencies CLOSER to 1/6 — not that each number lands exactly 100 times.
